title: Separating words problem
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), \[s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}\min\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\}.\]
why: Determining this scale would quantify how little finite-state memory suffices to distinguish an arbitrary pair of long binary strings.
status_note: The checked 2026 preprints retain a general one-third-power upper-bound scale and do not give matching asymptotics or a universal logarithmic bound. Read on 13 September 2026; proofs were not independently verified and the literature search was bounded.

progress.text: The source poses a logarithmic upper-bound target and mentions a one-third-power bound as an intermediate scale.
Bathie reports the general one-third-power upper-bound frontier and proves a different guarantee for a random word against an adversarial comparison word.
Xu’s preprint abstract gives an elementary proof of an \(O(n^{1/3}(\log n)^{7/3})\)-state upper bound.

importance.reason: A basic state-complexity problem measuring finite automata’s ability to distinguish arbitrary strings and connecting to reconstruction questions.

sentences: The problem measures the smallest deterministic automaton that distinguishes two binary words of equal length.
A different automaton may be chosen for each pair and its behavior on other words is unrestricted.
The target is the worst-case number of states as a function of the common word length.
The original question proposes a logarithmic upper bound, while recent general bounds have a one-third power with logarithmic factors.
The benchmark asks for matching constant-factor asymptotics across all pairs, not a random-input guarantee.

definitions: The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton. A proposed positive comparison function \(f\) determines the requested asymptotic scale when constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) exist with \(a f(n)\le s(n)\le b f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). The source’s conjectured endpoint is \(s(n)=O(\log n)\); the card explicitly asks for the underlying worst-case scale rather than asserting this endpoint.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function \(f(n)\) and a Lean proof of both constant-factor inequalities in the definitions. A universal small-DFA upper bound must be accompanied by a matching worst-case lower bound. This is asymptotic state complexity; the numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to big-O bounds. Results for random words or selected families of pairs do not determine the unrestricted maximum.

context_blocks.text: The original problem asks whether logarithmically many states always suffice to distinguish two equal-length binary words. This card develops that threshold question into determination of the worst-case state function.

The August 2026 primary abstract reports a general \(\widetilde O(n^{1/3})\) upper bound and studies a stronger result only when one word is random. The September preprint supplies another proof at the general one-third exponent, not a logarithmic universal bound.
